title: The Lantern Ferry Won't Wait
audienceRationale: A nine-year-old who aced rehearsed multiplication needs a world where recall is insufficient and construction is mandatory. Drag-to-build with a live product readout externalizes equal-groups thinking without teaching it mid-item; irreversible commits and countable consequences make the math feel consequential rather than quizzed. The addition trap, the constraint-selected factor pair, and the tarp crossing each remove one crutch (surface cues, memorized pairs, countable objects) in sequence, which is exactly the deepening-challenge shape a fast, confident finisher can respect. The five-departure structure gives the run a real cost — the Planner asked that this quest cost something — while the no-blame dockmaster keeps failure survivable.
openingPromise: Night is falling over the festival river. Five villages across the water are dark, waiting for their lanterns. You are the new dock loader, and the ferry captain rings the bell: "Load it right and load it fast — the ferry won't wait, and the water is rising." The promise: every crossing you load correctly lights another village on the far shore, and if you load all five, the whole river ignites in a chain of floating festival lights.
firstThreeSeconds: The screen opens already in motion: the ferry bumps against the dock, lantern crates slide down a chute onto the loading platform, water laps at the planks, and the dockmaster shouts the first order in a single speech bubble ("60 lanterns ordered — each crate holds 12"). A glowing empty crate-stack outline pulses on the ferry deck. No menu, no tutorial screen — the child's cursor is already a rope-hook hovering over the crates.
firstAction: The child grabs the rope-hook and drags crates from the chute onto the loading pallet one at a time; a running counter on the pallet shows crates × per-crate = current total in large glowing numerals that update with every crate added or removed. When the child believes the pallet matches the order, they drag the whole crate stack onto the ferry deck. That drag is the commit — the gangplank retracts and the ferry pulls away with whatever is aboard.
interactionDemonstration: Concrete walkthrough of Crossing 4: the bell rings, the dockmaster shouts "36 for the bridge village — ramp's exactly six crates wide!" The child drags crates onto the deck grid. Suppose they build 4 rows of 9 from memory: the readout shows 4 × 9 = 36 in glowing chalk — the total is right — but when they commit-drag the stack, the 9-wide rows clip the ramp posts, three crates per row tumble into the water, and the stack slides back to the pallet before boarding (this pre-board jam is a physical constraint check, not a hint about the math; the readout still shows their arithmetic was 36). The child must now reason which factor pair of 36 is at most 6 wide, rebuild as 6 × 6, watch the readout confirm 36 again, and commit. The stack clears the ramp posts with inches to spare, the gangplank snaps up, the double-bell rings, and the bridge village's lantern chain ignites arch by arch across the actual bridge. Verbatim capture records the final committed arrangement (6×6), the earlier jammed attempt (4×9), and latency from order reveal to successful commit.
coreInteraction: Build-then-commit loading. Each crossing states a total and one known part of the grouping (per-crate count, crate count, rows, or a ramp constraint). The child constructs the missing part physically: dragging crates to set a count, arranging crates into rows × columns on the deck grid, or (in the tarp crossing) typing/dialing the missing factor on the dock manifest when no objects are visible to count. The live product readout on the pallet is the only feedback before commit — it shows what the child has built, never whether it is right. Committing is always the same gesture: drag the stack aboard, the ferry leaves, and the far shore reveals the truth. No hints, no confirmation dialog, no undo after the gangplank lifts. Each response is captured verbatim with latency from problem-reveal to commit.
mathAsPower: Multiplication is the loading arm itself. The child never selects an answer from options — the number of crates dragged IS the missing factor, the arrangement of rows × columns IS the factor pair, and the product readout IS the world's physics. Load 5 crates of 12 and the readout shows 60 and the ferry sits at the right waterline; load 6 and the ferry visibly rides lower, overweight. On the constraint crossing, a 9-wide crate arrangement physically will not fit the 6-wide ramp — the crates clip the ramp posts and tumble back, so only the factor pair that satisfies the situation can even board. On the tarp crossing, the child's dialed factor determines how many crate-shaped bulges appear under the tarp when the ferry departs. Correct multiplication makes villages light up, lantern chains ignite across the water, and the river current itself glows brighter. Wrong multiplication is equally physical: too few crates and a village stays half-dark with visible unlit houses equal to the shortfall; too many and surplus crates float back downstream past the child on the next crossing.
stakes: Each crossing lights or fails to light a real village visible on the far shore, and the water rises one plank after every crossing regardless of outcome — the dock is sinking on a fixed clock of five departures. The final village hosts the festival finale: if it stays dark, the closing lantern-release happens without them. Stakes are concrete, visible, and cumulative, but never punitive to the child's identity — it is villages, not scores, that go dark.
consequences: After a wrong commit the ferry still leaves — the world does not pause to correct the child. At the far shore the dockmaster reports plainly what actually arrived and what didn't: "48 lanterns landed. The village needed 60. Twelve houses on the hill stay dark tonight." The camera shows exactly those twelve unlit houses. If the child added instead of multiplied on Crossing 3, the dockmaster counts the dark boats aloud. If the wrong factor pair jammed on the ramp in Crossing 4, the crates that tumbled are shown bobbing downstream. No explanation of the correct math is given — only the true consequence in the world. Then the water rises a plank and the next crossing begins immediately.
recovery: There is no retry within a crossing — commits are final, matching the evidence contract's unassisted-verbatim requirement. Recovery is narrative and forward-facing: after the run, any darkened village sends a rowboat asking for a "moonlight delivery," an optional replay of the full five-crossing run with freshly authored numbers (never the same pairs). Emotionally, the dockmaster never blames the child — he blames the tide, the manifest ink, the hurry — keeping the child willing to attempt the next crossing at full effort rather than deflating after a miss.
progression: Crossing 1 — Missing crate count: Dockmaster: "The first village ordered 60 lanterns. Each crate holds 12." Child drags crates until the pallet reads the right stack, then commits. Tests missing factor with unseen pair 12×5; pure equal-groups recovery, generous deck space, no constraints.

Crossing 2 — Total under a row constraint: Dockmaster: "7 crates arrived, 8 lanterns each — tell the far dock how many lanterns are coming. But this deck only fits crates in rows of 4." Child must state/build the total (56) AND arrange 7 crates as rows-of-4 on the deck grid, discovering the arrangement doesn't tile evenly (one row of 3) — the product survives the messy arrangement, separating total-finding from tidy-array dependence.

Crossing 3 — Addition trap word problem: Dockmaster, casually: "Nine families are waiting on the east bank, and each family needs 7 lanterns for their boat." The numbers 9 and 7 sit side by side begging to be added to 16. The pallet readout will happily show a 16-lantern load — the ferry departs light, and 47 boats stay dark if the child adds. Tests word-problem interpretation: recognizing equal-groups structure in narrative with no array pictured.

Crossing 4 — Factor pair selected by constraint: "36 lanterns for the bridge village — and the ramp is exactly 6 crates wide, no crate may hang over." 36 factors as 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6; the child may know 4×9 cold from practice, but a 4-wide or 9-wide stack physically jams on the ramp. Only 6 rows of 6 boards. A memorized pair fails; the situation selects the factor.

Crossing 5 — The tarp: "The last load is already lashed under the tarp: 84 lanterns in rows of 12. The manifest needs the row count before we cast off." Nothing to drag or count — the deck grid is hidden. The child dials the missing factor (7) directly on the manifest wheel and commits by dragging the sealed tarp-stack aboard. Largest numbers of the run, zero countable objects, pure missing-factor reasoning under the highest stakes: this village hosts the festival finale.
interactionContinuity: One gesture grammar carries the whole run: grab, build, commit-drag. Crossing 1 introduces it in its simplest form; Crossings 2–4 add arrangement and constraint to the same gesture; Crossing 5 keeps the identical commit-drag but replaces countable building with the manifest wheel, so the final and hardest item still feels like the same job. Between crossings there is no scene break — the ferry returns, the water rises, the next order is shouted. The child never leaves the dock, never sees a menu, and the dockmaster's voice is the only narrator from bell to finale.
worldReaction: Every loaded crate changes the ferry's waterline in real time — overloads ride low and slow, underloads ride high and fast. Correct deliveries ignite a lantern chain that arcs from the village into the river, and by the fifth correct crossing the five chains meet mid-river in a spiral. Wrong deliveries leave countable darkness: unlit houses, dark boats, drifting surplus crates that reappear on later crossings as flotsam. The rising water swallows one dock plank per crossing, ratcheting urgency without a timer bar. The world never says "correct" or "incorrect" — it only shows what the numbers did.
payoff: If all five villages light, the festival finale triggers: hundreds of lanterns release simultaneously from every shore, reflect in the water, and spell the child's loader rank ("Master Loader of the Five Crossings") in floating lights. A partial run earns a proportional finale — three villages lit means three lantern chains, visibly beautiful but visibly incomplete, which motivates the moonlight-delivery replay honestly rather than through shame. The dockmaster hands over a stamped manifest showing each crossing's order and what was delivered, letting the child see their own run as a record.
replayVariation: Replays ("moonlight deliveries") regenerate all five crossings from templates with fresh unseen number pairs and rotated constraint types: the addition-trap wording changes surface story (families/boats becomes stalls/flags), the multi-factor total changes (36 → 48 or 40) with a different physical constraint (ramp width → crane weight limit per row), and the tarp crossing swaps which part is hidden (rows given/columns hidden vs. total given under tarp with per-crate known). Night palette shifts to moonlight silver, and the dockmaster's dialogue acknowledges it's the second run. No number pair or word-problem surface ever repeats verbatim.
visualDirection: Warm dusk palette sliding toward deep indigo night across the five crossings, so the world itself darkens as stakes rise and lit villages matter more. Lanterns are the light source of the whole scene — paper-warm amber against cold water. Chunky, readable crates with painted lantern counts on their sides; the deck grid is bold rope-line squares a nine-year-old can parse instantly. The pallet's live product readout is rendered as glowing chalk on a dock slate, large and central. Water is stylized with visible current lines that brighten with each successful delivery. Silhouetted villages on the far shore have individually countable windows so consequences are literally countable. UI chrome is nearly absent: the world is the interface.
motionDirection: Everything drags with weight: crates have a heavy, satisfying pickup-tilt and land with a settle-bounce; the ferry lists physically under load. The commit drag is the signature motion — the whole stack slides aboard, the gangplank snaps up, and the ferry pulls away with wake ripples, an irreversible departure the child feels. Rising water creeps up planks in slow, ominous increments between crossings. Lantern chains ignite in a traveling spark that races along the string. On the tarp crossing, the tarp breathes gently over its hidden cargo, and the manifest wheel clicks with detented rotation. Wrong-load consequences animate calmly, not violently: crates bob away, houses simply never light.
soundDirection: A quiet river-night bed: water lapping, distant festival murmur, crickets. Each crate drag has a rope-creak and wooden thunk; the live readout updating gives a soft chalk-scratch tick. The ferry bell rings once at each order reveal and twice at departure — the departure double-ring is the audio signature of commitment. Correct deliveries earn a swelling lantern-chime cascade pitched higher with each lit village; wrong deliveries get no sting or buzzer, just the absence of chimes and the dockmaster's plain spoken report over quieter water. Rising water gets a low creak-and-slosh. The finale is a full chime-and-crowd swell. Never a wrong-answer punishment sound — the world stays dignified.
usefulLibraries: PixiJS (2D WebGL rendering for water, lantern glow, and crate sprites)
GSAP (drag physics feel, ferry departure and waterline tweens, lantern chain ignition sequences)
Howler.js (layered ambient bed, positional chimes, bell cues)
interact.js or PixiJS built-in pointer events (drag-and-drop of crates and commit stack)
simplex-noise (water surface shimmer and current lines)
engagementPrediction: The child previously finished a paced challenge in 43 seconds, rated it 5/5, and left without replaying — consistent with enjoying pace but finding no reason to return. Prediction: this run takes 4–7 minutes because commits are physical and irreversible, latency per crossing rises from Crossing 1 to Crossing 5 (especially 4 and 5), and the child completes all five crossings without abandonment. If any village goes dark, predicted probability of accepting the moonlight-delivery replay is meaningfully higher than the prior zero-replay observation, because incompleteness is visible in the finale rather than reported as a score.
falsifyingEvidence: The design fails if: (a) commit latency on Crossings 4–5 is not longer than on Crossing 1 (the removed crutches added no strain); (b) the child abandons before Crossing 5 or shows frustration signals absent from baseline (the cost overshot); (c) the child solves Crossing 4 by dragging arrangements trial-and-error against the ramp until one fits, with readout thrash and no pre-commit pause (the world let physical fiddling substitute for factor reasoning); (d) the addition trap catches the child but the identical structure re-catches them on replay with new surfaces (consequence display taught nothing); or (e) fun rating drops below 4 with all five crossings correct (the challenge read as tedium, not stakes).
